q1.prompt: You run AI_SENTIMENT(comment)['categories'][0]['sentiment']::STRING and get the value negative. What does this mean?

a.text: The AI classified the comment text as having a negative overall tone
a.feedback: Correct! AI_SENTIMENT returns a structured object; the sentiment category is at ['categories'][0]['sentiment']. The value is one of: positive, negative, neutral, or mixed.

b.text: The customer gave a negative numeric score (1 or 2)
b.feedback: The numeric score column and the AI sentiment are separate signals. AI_SENTIMENT reads the text content, not the score column — they often agree but can differ.

c.text: The comment contains profanity or inappropriate content
c.feedback: AI_SENTIMENT measures emotional tone (positive/negative/neutral/mixed), not content appropriateness. Use AI_FILTER for content moderation.

d.text: The AI couldn't parse the comment and returned an error code
d.feedback: 'negative' is a valid sentiment category, not an error. If parsing failed, the function would return null, not a category string.

q2.prompt: You run AI_CLASSIFY(comment, ['Slow Service', 'Product Quality', 'Pricing', 'Other']). How do you extract the chosen label from the result?

a.feedback: Correct! AI_CLASSIFY returns a structured object; the winning label is at ['labels'][0]. Cast to STRING to use it as a plain text value.

b.feedback: The key is 'labels', not 'category'. Use result['labels'][0]::STRING to get the chosen label.

c.feedback: Casting the whole object to STRING gives you raw JSON text, not the label. You need to navigate to the 'labels' key first.

d.feedback: 'sentiment' is the key used by AI_SENTIMENT, not AI_CLASSIFY. AI_CLASSIFY uses 'labels'.

q3.prompt: Why is it better to CREATE TABLE AS SELECT (CTAS) with AI functions rather than calling them in every dashboard query?

a.text: AI functions bill per token — running them once and persisting the result avoids re-charging for the same computation on every query
a.feedback: Correct! This is the 'compute once, query many times' pattern. AI functions cost credits each time they process tokens, so pre-computing and saving to a table is far more cost-efficient than calling them in live queries.

b.text: AI functions are not allowed inside dashboard tools — they can only run in notebooks
b.feedback: AI functions can be called anywhere SQL runs, including dashboards. The reason to persist is cost and latency, not a technical restriction.

c.text: CTAS is required because AI functions only work on full table scans
c.feedback: AI functions work on any row set — you can LIMIT or filter. The CTAS pattern is about cost efficiency, not a scan requirement.

d.text: Dashboard tools can't read Snowflake views, so the data must be in a table
d.feedback: Dashboards read views fine. The reason to persist AI results is to avoid re-running expensive AI calls on every query refresh.

q1.prompt: AI_EXTRACT(description, ['origin_country', 'roast_level']) returns a result. How do you access the origin_country value from it?

a.feedback: Correct! AI_EXTRACT wraps its output under a 'response' key. Navigate to it with semi-colon path notation: result:response:field_name::STRING.

b.feedback: Close — but there's an extra level. AI_EXTRACT puts its fields under a 'response' key, so the path is result:response:origin_country::STRING.

c.feedback: Bracket notation works for some JSON paths, but AI_EXTRACT nests its fields under a 'response' key first: result:response:origin_country::STRING.

d.feedback: Casting the whole object to STRING gives you raw JSON text. You need to navigate into the 'response' key to reach individual extracted fields.

q2.prompt: You run AI_EMBED('snowflake-arctic-embed-m-v1.5', description)::VECTOR(FLOAT, 768). What is the output and what is it used for?

a.text: A 768-dimensional numeric vector representing the semantic meaning of the text — used for similarity search and clustering
a.feedback: Correct! Embeddings convert text into a fixed-size numeric vector. Similar texts produce vectors that are close together, enabling VECTOR_COSINE_SIMILARITY and Cortex Search to find semantically related content.

b.text: A 768-character text summary of the description
b.feedback: Embeddings are not text summaries — they're numeric vectors. Use AI_COMPLETE for text generation and summarization.

c.text: A hash of the description for deduplication
c.feedback: Hashes are fixed-length identifiers for exact matching. Embeddings are numeric vectors designed to measure semantic similarity, not identity.

d.text: A classification label chosen from 768 possible categories
d.feedback: 768 is the vector dimension, not the number of categories. Use AI_CLASSIFY if you need categorical labels.

q3.prompt: What is the key advantage of using a Dynamic Table over a plain CTAS for an AI enrichment pipeline?

a.text: A Dynamic Table automatically refreshes and runs AI functions only on new or changed rows — avoiding the cost of re-processing the whole table
a.feedback: Correct! A CTAS is a one-time snapshot — every refresh re-processes every row and re-pays the AI token cost. A Dynamic Table tracks changes and only processes the delta, which saves tokens and time as the dataset grows.

b.text: A Dynamic Table runs faster because it stores data in a compressed format
b.feedback: The performance advantage isn't compression — it's incremental processing. Only new/changed rows trigger AI function calls, not the whole table.

c.text: Dynamic Tables don't require a warehouse, so they eliminate compute costs
c.feedback: Dynamic Tables do require a warehouse (set via WAREHOUSE in the CREATE statement). The saving is in AI token costs — not compute costs.

d.text: Dynamic Tables automatically translate the output into multiple languages
d.feedback: Language translation is done by AI_TRANSLATE. Dynamic Tables are a scheduling/incremental-refresh mechanism, not a transformation function.

q1.prompt: You run AI_REDACT(comment) on a customer feedback table. What happens to the original data in the source table?

a.text: Nothing — AI_REDACT is non-destructive and only transforms the output at query time; the source table is unchanged
a.feedback: Correct! AI_REDACT applies redaction in the query result only. The underlying table still holds the original text, so authorized roles can still see the unredacted data by querying the source directly.

b.text: PII is permanently deleted from the source table rows
b.feedback: AI_REDACT does not modify the source table. It's a query-time transformation — the original data is preserved, which is important for authorized users who still need access.

c.text: The source table is locked until the redaction job completes
c.feedback: AI_REDACT is a SQL function, not a batch job. It runs row-by-row at query time and doesn't lock the source table.

d.text: PII is replaced with nulls in the source table
d.feedback: Nulls would be a destructive change to the source. AI_REDACT replaces PII with placeholders like [NAME] only in the query output — the source remains untouched.

q2.prompt: AI_FILTER(PROMPT('This comment is appropriate for a business report: {0}', comment)) returns FALSE for a row. What does this mean?

a.text: The AI evaluated the condition as false — the comment does NOT meet the criteria 'appropriate for a business report'
a.feedback: Correct! AI_FILTER returns TRUE or FALSE based on whether the natural-language condition is satisfied. A FALSE result means the AI judged that this comment should be excluded by the filter.

b.text: The function failed to process the comment and returned an error code
b.feedback: FALSE is a valid result, not an error. AI_FILTER always returns TRUE or FALSE (or null if the input is null). An error would be an exception, not a boolean.

c.text: The comment is empty or null
c.feedback: A null input would return null, not FALSE. FALSE means the AI actively evaluated the condition and determined it was not satisfied.

d.text: The comment was flagged as containing profanity and must be deleted
d.feedback: AI_FILTER only returns a boolean — it doesn't trigger any deletion. Acting on the result (filtering out rows, alerting, etc.) is up to the query logic around it.

q3.prompt: As a Platform Admin, you want to prevent your account from using large expensive models while still allowing AI functions. What is the correct approach?

a.text: Revoke CORTEX-MODEL-ROLE-ALL from PUBLIC and grant only specific CORTEX-MODEL-ROLE-<model> roles for the approved models
a.feedback: Correct! By default, CORTEX-MODEL-ROLE-ALL is granted to PUBLIC, giving everyone access to all models. Revoking it and granting only specific model roles lets you allow small models like 'llama3.1-8b' while blocking larger, more expensive ones.

b.text: Revoke the SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_USER database role from all roles — this disables all AI functions
b.feedback: Revoking CORTEX_USER would disable ALL AI functions for those roles, not just expensive models. Model RBAC (CORTEX-MODEL-ROLE-* application roles) lets you keep AI functions enabled but restrict which models can be used.

c.text: Set a budget alert threshold in ACCOUNT_USAGE — Snowflake will automatically block AI calls when the threshold is hit
c.feedback: Budget alerts notify you about spending but don't automatically block calls. Model RBAC application roles proactively restrict which models can be used before any spend occurs.

d.text: Grant SNOWFLAKE.CORTEX_EMBED_USER instead of CORTEX_USER — this blocks text generation models
d.feedback: CORTEX_EMBED_USER limits users to embedding only (AI_EMBED). But if users already have CORTEX_USER, you'd need to revoke it — and this approach is per-role, not account-wide. Model RBAC (revoking CORTEX-MODEL-ROLE-ALL and granting specific model roles) is the right tool for restricting specific models globally.
